lessons.title: سلام (salâm) — hello, one joined word at a time

segments.text: Persian runs right to left. Start at the right edge of سلام (salâm). Its four letters are س s, ل l, ا long â, and م m:
س, ل, ا, م becomes salâm.

The shapes touch because Persian letters usually join inside a word. The tall ا does not join to the letter after it, so the final م begins a new stroke group. You do not need the rest of the alphabet yet.

salâm means “hello” and literally evokes peace. Persian borrowed it from Arabic, where the consonants s-l-m organize a family concerned with peace, safety, and wholeness. That same old Semitic family also includes Hebrew shalom. The word is now thoroughly everyday Persian.
Say salâm to one person or a group. It is neutral, friendly, and safe in most situations.
See a neighbor: Salâm!
Answer a greeting: Salâm!
Read سلام from right to left. Which letter makes the long â? ا. Now say the word once without looking: salâm.
Persian Online: the writing system.
You already know final م m from سلام (salâm). In ممنون (mamnun), it appears first, on the right. Read the visible consonants right to left:
م, م, ن, و, ن becomes mamnun.
Persian normally leaves short vowels unwritten, so the first a is something you learn with the word. و supplies the long u sound here. Its sound can change in other words; today, it is simply u.

mamnun literally describes someone as grateful or obliged, and in ordinary conversation it works as “thanks.” Persian received the word from Arabic. Its consonant family is m-n-n, associated in Arabic with favor or kindness.
A: سلام — salâm — Hello.
B: سلام — salâm — Hello.
A: ممنون — mamnun — Thank you.
Do not add a new grammar rule. Treat mamnun as one useful social move.
Which direction do you read? Right to left. Which visible letter carries long u here? و. Say: salâm — mamnun.
Read بله (bale) from right to left: ب b, ل l, ه h. Persian does not normally print the short vowels, but speakers supply them:
ب, ل, ه becomes bale becomes yes.

The last ه is written even though careful speech ends with a light vowel sound rather than a strong English h. Listen for the whole word; do not force every letter to sound identical in every position.
bale is a standard, polite “yes.” A more casual âre exists, but one clear affirmative is enough for this lesson.
“Is this Persian?” — Bale.
“Are you ready?” — Bale, mamnun. — Yes, thank you.
Cover the romanization. Read بله. Which sounds are not written as separate letters? The short a and e. Answer once: bale.
You know final ه from بله (bale). Add ن n on its right:
ن, ه becomes na becomes no.
The short a is understood rather than printed. The same ن appeared inside ممنون (mamnun), so this is mostly recognition, not a fresh alphabet lesson.

Persian na belongs to an old Indo-Iranian negative family. Related forms turn up across Iranian and Indo-Aryan languages. That bridge will be useful when you compare Persian with Hindi or Urdu, but for now the job is simple: bale affirms; na rejects.
بله — bale — yes.
نه — na — no.
Say the pair twice, changing only the answer: bale — na.
Read نه from right to left. Which first sound does ن make? n. Answer “no” in Persian: na.
